claim: During deep anesthesia, the electroencephalographic (EEG) signal of the brain alternates between bursts of activity and periods of relative silence (suppressions).
source: During deep anesthesia, the electroencephalographic (EEG) signal of the brain alternates between bursts of activity and periods of relative silence (suppressions).
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of burst-suppression based on existing scientific knowledge and literature.

claim: The origin of burst-suppression and its distribution across the brain remain matters of debate.
source: The origin of burst-suppression and its distribution across the brain remain matters of debate.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific understanding and open questions in the field.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was used to map the brain areas involved in anesthesia-induced burst-suppression across four mammalian species: humans, long-tailed macaques, common marmosets, and rats.
source: In this work, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to map the brain areas involved in anesthesia-induced burst-suppression across four mammalian species: humans, long-tailed macaques, common marmosets, and rats.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Distinct burst-suppression signatures were found in all four species studied.
source: Applying this method to animal fMRI datasets, we found distinct burst-suppression signatures in all species.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: In rats, the entire neocortex engaged in burst-suppression.
source: The burst-suppression maps revealed a marked inter-species difference: in rats, the entire neocortex engaged in burst-suppression, while in primates most sensory areas were excluded—predominantly the primary visual cortex.
evidence: This is a key finding from the fMRI mapping data.

claim: In primates, most sensory areas were excluded from burst-suppression, predominantly the primary visual cortex.
source: The burst-suppression maps revealed a marked inter-species difference: in rats, the entire neocortex engaged in burst-suppression, while in primates most sensory areas were excluded—predominantly the primary visual cortex.
evidence: This is a key finding from the fMRI mapping data showing inter-species differences.

claim: Most anesthetics lead to a dose-dependent transition from mild sedation to deep unconsciousness, accompanied by a progression of distinct electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns.
source: Most anesthetics lead to a dose-dependent transition from mild sedation to deep unconsciousness, accompanied by a progression of distinct electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns (Brown et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Low isoflurane concentrations lead to high-amplitude low-frequency activity.
source: Low isoflurane concentrations lead to high-amplitude low-frequency activity, whereas at higher concentrations, the ongoing activity is quasi-periodically interrupted by quiescent periods that can last from seconds to minutes.
evidence: This describes known effects of isoflurane based on established knowledge.

claim: At higher isoflurane concentrations, the ongoing activity is quasi-periodically interrupted by quiescent periods that can last from seconds to minutes.
source: Low isoflurane concentrations lead to high-amplitude low-frequency activity, whereas at higher concentrations, the ongoing activity is quasi-periodically interrupted by quiescent periods that can last from seconds to minutes.
evidence: This describes the characteristic pattern of burst-suppression under isoflurane.

claim: The alternation between bursts of activity and gaps of quiescence is termed burst-suppression.
source: This alternation between bursts of activity and gaps of quiescence is termed burst-suppression (Swank, 1949; Swank and Watson, 1949).
evidence: This is a definition supported by historical citations.

claim: As anesthesia deepens, suppression periods become longer and ultimately culminate in complete electrical silence.
source: As anesthesia deepens, suppression periods become longer and ultimately culminate in complete electrical silence.
evidence: This describes the progression of burst-suppression with increasing anesthetic depth.

claim: The same sequence of burst-suppression unfolds for many other anesthetics.
source: The same sequence unfolds for many other anesthetics (Akrawi et al., 1996; Fleischmann et al., 2018) and even during deep hypothermia (Westover et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on various anesthetics.

claim: Burst-suppression appears during deep hypothermia.
source: The same sequence unfolds for many other anesthetics (Akrawi et al., 1996; Fleischmann et al., 2018) and even during deep hypothermia (Westover et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on hypothermia.

claim: Burst-suppression appears in comas of various etiologies, for which it holds diagnostic and prognostic value.
source: Burst-suppression also appears in comas of various etiologies, for which it holds diagnostic and prognostic value (Brenner, 1985; Brown et al., 2010; Cloostermans et al., 2012; Hofmeijer et al., 2014; Young, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Burst-suppression is often used as the target EEG pattern for intended neuroprotection as well as pharmacological control of intracranial hypertension.
source: Clinically, burst-suppression is often used as the target EEG pattern for intended neuroprotection as well as pharmacological control of intracranial hypertension (An et al., 2015; Westover et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes clinical applications supported by citations.

claim: Some researchers propose that burst-suppression represents a common low-order 'attractor' state—a hallmark of a profoundly inactive brain.
source: The presence of burst-suppression in a variety of unconscious conditions has led some researchers to propose that it represents a common low-order 'attractor' state—a hallmark of a profoundly inactive brain (Ching et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation from the cited literature.

claim: Several models have focused on the temporal bistability of burst-suppression.
source: Several models have focused on the temporal bistability (Bojak et al., 2015; Ching et al., 2012; Kroeger and Amzica, 2007; Liley and Walsh, 2013), while many open questions surround the spatial properties of bursts—namely, their origin and propagation across brain areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Many open questions surround the spatial properties of bursts—namely, their origin and propagation across brain areas.
source: Several models have focused on the temporal bistability (Bojak et al., 2015; Ching et al., 2012; Kroeger and Amzica, 2007; Liley and Walsh, 2013), while many open questions surround the spatial properties of bursts—namely, their origin and propagation across brain areas.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Bursts have traditionally been viewed as globally synchronous events, based on their simultaneous occurrence across EEG electrodes.
source: Bursts have traditionally been viewed as globally synchronous events, based on their simultaneous occurrence across EEG electrodes (Clark and Rosner, 1973; Swank, 1949).
evidence: This describes a traditional view supported by historical citations.

claim: Recent findings from electrocorticogram in humans and widefield calcium imaging in rats have challenged the view of bursts as globally synchronous events by demonstrating considerable spatial variation in burst origin and propagation.
source: However, recent findings from electrocorticogram in humans (Lewis et al., 2013) and widefield calcium imaging in rats (Ming et al., 2020) have challenged this view by demonstrating considerable spatial variation in burst origin and propagation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: It is yet unclear whether burst-suppression is intrinsically cortical or is influenced by subcortical sources.
source: Furthermore, it is yet unclear whether burst-suppression is intrinsically cortical or is influenced by subcortical sources.
evidence: This identifies an open question in the field.

claim: According to one hypothesis, the cortex spontaneously falls into burst-suppression upon anatomical or functional disconnection from other brain areas.
source: According to one hypothesis, the cortex spontaneously falls into burst-suppression upon anatomical or functional disconnection from other brain areas.
evidence: This presents a hypothesis about the mechanism of burst-suppression.

claim: Burst-suppression has been observed in isolated neocortical slice preparations.
source: This view is supported by observations of burst-suppression in isolated neocortical slice preparations (Lukatch et al., 2005; Lukatch and MacIver, 1996), but contradicted by the ability of sensory stimuli to evoke bursts indistinguishable from the spontaneously occurring ones (Hartikainen et al., 1995; Hudetz and Imas, 2007; Kroeger and Amzica, 2007; Land et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Sensory stimuli can evoke bursts indistinguishable from the spontaneously occurring ones.
source: This view is supported by observations of burst-suppression in isolated neocortical slice preparations (Lukatch et al., 2005; Lukatch and MacIver, 1996), but contradicted by the ability of sensory stimuli to evoke bursts indistinguishable from the spontaneously occurring ones (Hartikainen et al., 1995; Hudetz and Imas, 2007; Kroeger and Amzica, 2007; Land et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The two distinct phases of burst-suppression correspond to different energy consumption levels, which should—through neurovascular coupling—translate into noticeable changes in blood flow and oxygenation.
source: The two distinct phases of burst-suppression correspond to different energy consumption levels, which should—through neurovascular coupling—translate into noticeable changes in blood flow and oxygenation (Hillman, 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on neurovascular coupling principles, supported by a citation.

claim: In rats, bursts are coupled with strong hemodynamic responses as shown by a combination of EEG with optical imaging of cerebral blood flow.
source: In rats, a combination of EEG with optical imaging of cerebral blood flow revealed that bursts are coupled with strong hemodynamic responses (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The same effect of bursts being coupled with hemodynamic responses was demonstrated in macaques and humans using simultaneous EEG-fMRI.
source: The same effect was demonstrated in macaques (Zhang et al., 2019) and humans (Golkowski et al., 2017) using simultaneous EEG-fMRI.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The burst timing from EEG can be used for fMRI mapping of burst-suppression.
source: These two studies have shown that the burst timing from EEG can be used for fMRI mapping of burst-suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies.

claim: About four of five animal fMRI studies are conducted under anesthesia, most commonly with isoflurane.
source: About four of five such studies are conducted under anesthesia, most commonly with isoflurane (Mandino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statistical observation supported by a citation.

claim: Medium-to-high concentrations of isoflurane lead to burst-suppression.
source: Given that medium-to-high concentrations of isoflurane lead to burst-suppression (Kroeger et al., 2013), we hypothesized that many animal fMRI experiments have been conducted during this state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and forms the basis for a hypothesis.

claim: Many animal fMRI experiments have been conducted during burst-suppression.
source: Given that medium-to-high concentrations of isoflurane lead to burst-suppression (Kroeger et al., 2013), we hypothesized that many animal fMRI experiments have been conducted during this state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from known facts.

claim: Global BOLD signal synchronization has been reported in isoflurane-anesthetized animals.
source: This assumption is supported by reports of global BOLD signal synchronization in isoflurane-anesthetized animals (Kalthoff et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Paasonen et al., 2018), as is expected during burst-suppression (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Global BOLD signal synchronization is expected during burst-suppression.
source: This assumption is supported by reports of global BOLD signal synchronization in isoflurane-anesthetized animals (Kalthoff et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Paasonen et al., 2018), as is expected during burst-suppression (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an expectation based on a cited study.

claim: Animal fMRI researchers typically try to avoid the confounding effect of burst-suppression by using low concentrations of isoflurane.
source: Animal fMRI researchers typically try to avoid this confounding effect by using low concentrations of isoflurane (Liu et al., 2013), opting for different anesthetic regimes (Kalthoff et al., 2013; Paasonen et al., 2018), or applying global signal regression during fMRI preprocessing (Kalthoff et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes common practices supported by citations.

claim: 19 out of 20 human subjects exhibited the typical bistable EEG alternation at high sevoflurane concentration (3.9–4.6%).
source: The high sevoflurane concentration had been intentionally chosen in the initial study to induce burst-suppression (Ranft et al., 2016), and indeed 19/20 subjects exhibited the typical bistable EEG alternation at this concentration (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a data observation from the study.

claim: 4 out of 20 human subjects exhibited burst-suppression at the intermediate sevoflurane concentration (3%), albeit with shorter suppression phases.
source: The same applied to 4/20 subjects at the intermediate concentration, albeit with shorter suppression phases.
evidence: This is a data observation from the study.

claim: The remaining intermediate-concentration recordings as well as all low-concentration recordings showed uninterrupted slow-wave EEG activity.
source: The remaining intermediate-concentration recordings as well as all low-concentration recordings showed uninterrupted slow-wave EEG activity.
evidence: This is a data observation from the study.

claim: The results are consistent with the known dose-dependency of burst-suppression.
source: These results are consistent with the known dose-dependency of burst-suppression (Pilge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by a citation.

claim: fMRI runs with EEG-defined burst-suppression showed pronounced signal fluctuations that spanned almost the entire cortex.
source: Upon examining carpet plots from fMRI runs with EEG-defined burst-suppression, we identified pronounced signal fluctuations that spanned almost the entire cortex (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a data observation from the study, with reference to a figure.

claim: fMRI runs with continuous slow-wave EEG activity showed no cortex-wide fluctuations.
source: Conversely, fMRI runs with continuous slow-wave EEG activity showed no such cortex-wide fluctuations (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a data observation from the study, with reference to a figure.

claim: In fMRI runs with cortex-wide fluctuations, the bistable pattern visible on the carpet plot was captured by one of the principal components—in most cases the first PC.
source: In fMRI runs with cortex-wide fluctuations, the bistable pattern visible on the carpet plot was captured by one of the principal components (PCs)—in most cases the first PC (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a data observation from the study, with reference to a figure.

claim: The asymmetric PC was strongly correlated with most cortical voxel time series.
source: This component was strongly correlated with most cortical voxel time series (Figure 1E), shifting the histogram of Pearson's correlation coefficients (r) away from zero—unlike the symmetric zero-centered histograms of other PCs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a data observation from the study, with reference to figures.

claim: Every run with EEG burst-suppression had a single PC with median r>0.45, which was not the case for any of the runs with continuous slow waves.
source: Every run with EEG burst-suppression had a single PC with median r>0.45, which was not the case for any of the runs with continuous slow waves.
evidence: This is a data observation demonstrating the discriminatory power of the asymmetric PC metric.

claim: A single recording (subject 15 at high sevoflurane concentration) exhibited no asymmetric PC despite showing EEG burst-suppression.
source: A single recording was an exception to this rule (subject 15 at high sevoflurane concentration, see Figure 1G), exhibiting no asymmetric PC.
evidence: This is a data observation noting an exception.

claim: The EEG of the exceptional recording (subject 15) showed near-constant suppression interrupted by only one short burst.
source: The EEG of this recording showed near-constant suppression interrupted by only one short burst.
evidence: This is a data observation explaining the exception.

claim: The asymmetric PC closely follows the alternating burst-suppression pattern of EEG.
source: Notably, this asymmetric PC closely follows the alternating burst-suppression pattern of EEG (Figure 1A–D) and likely is a direct hemodynamic correlate.
evidence: This is an inference from the data, with reference to figures.

claim: The BOLD signal of the asymmetric PCs was strongly correlated with the EEG-derived model (Pearson's r=0.73 ± 0.11, mean ± SD).
source: The BOLD signal of the asymmetric PCs was indeed strongly correlated with the EEG-derived model (Pearson's r=0.73 ± 0.11, mean ± SD), but with a notable time-lag between the two.
evidence: This is a quantitative data observation from the study.

claim: The asymmetric PC was delayed by 3.71 ± 2.22 s (mean ± SD) compared with the neurovascular model.
source: A cross-correlation analysis (Figure 1H) showed that the asymmetric PC was delayed by 3.71 ± 2.22 s (mean ± SD) compared with the neurovascular model.
evidence: This is a quantitative data observation from the study.

claim: The lag between the asymmetric PC and the neurovascular model can be attributed to a slowing of the HRF—an expected effect of anesthesia.
source: This lag can be attributed to a slowing of the HRF—an expected effect of anesthesia (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by a citation.

claim: When accounting for the time lag, the correlation between the asymmetric PC and the EEG-derived model increased to r=0.84 ± 0.06.
source: We accounted for this lag by comparing the asymmetric PCs to the EEG-derived models at the time lags that maximized their cross-correlation and found that the correlation increased to r=0.84 ± 0.06.
evidence: This is a quantitative data observation from the study.

claim: The spatial patterns of Z statistical maps from GLM analyses using asymmetric PCs and EEG-derived models were nearly identical (neighborhood cross-correlation r=0.96 ± 0.03).
source: As expected, the spatial patterns of the resulting Z statistical maps were nearly identical between the two analyses: neighborhood cross-correlation r=0.96 ± 0.03 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative data observation demonstrating equivalence of methods.

claim: The human group burst-suppression map revealed significant correlation with asymmetric PCs in the striatum and across most of the cortex, with the prominent exception of occipital areas in and around the calcarine sulcus—the location of primary visual cortex (V1).
source: The group map revealed significant correlation with asymmetric PCs (burst-suppression) in the striatum and across most of the cortex, with the prominent exception of occipital areas in and around the calcarine sulcus—the location of primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the group-level analysis.

claim: In addition to V1, several other cortical patches were non-correlated with burst-suppression in humans, including primary somatosensory and motor areas around the central sulcus, and auditory areas on the dorsal bank of superior temporal gyrus.
source: In addition to V1, several other cortical patches were non-correlated with burst-suppression. We visualized these on an inflated representation of the cortical surface (Figure 2C–D). Some of them overlapped with primary cortices: somatosensory and motor areas around the central sulcus, and auditory areas on the dorsal bank of superior temporal gyrus—including Heschl's gyrus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the group-level analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Additional inactive patches in humans included the subcallosal cortex (subgenual cingulate), the parahippocampal gyrus, and the border between the insula and the frontoparietal operculum.
source: Additional inactive patches included the subcallosal cortex (subgenual cingulate), the parahippocampal gyrus, and the border between the insula and the frontoparietal operculum.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the group-level analysis.

claim: Anterior and midline parts of the thalamus were significantly correlated with burst-suppression in humans.
source: Anterior and midline parts of the thalamus were significantly correlated with burst-suppression, whereas the posterior thalamic nuclei, the cerebellar cortex, the hippocampus, and the amygdala were, for the most part, not engaged.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the group-level analysis.

claim: The posterior thalamic nuclei, the cerebellar cortex, the hippocampus, and the amygdala were, for the most part, not engaged in burst-suppression in humans.
source: Anterior and midline parts of the thalamus were significantly correlated with burst-suppression, whereas the posterior thalamic nuclei, the cerebellar cortex, the hippocampus, and the amygdala were, for the most part, not engaged.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the group-level analysis.

claim: Significant anticorrelation with burst-suppression was observed at the ventricular borders in humans.
source: Intriguingly, we observed significant anticorrelation with burst-suppression at the ventricular borders.
evidence: This is a data observation from the study.

claim: The anticorrelation at ventricular borders likely relates to a cycle of ventricular shrinkage (during bursts) and expansion (during suppressions).
source: After a closer examination of this effect (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2), we believe it relates to a cycle of ventricular shrinkage (during bursts) and expansion (during suppressions).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on closer examination.

claim: The widespread hemodynamic fluctuations during burst-suppression may exert a 'pumping' effect on the ventricles.
source: The widespread hemodynamic fluctuations during burst-suppression may exert a 'pumping' effect on the ventricles—an explanation consistent with reports of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) oscillations during sleep (Fultz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to related work.

claim: 13 macaques were anesthetized with isoflurane (concentration range 0.95–1.5%) and mechanically ventilated.
source: The 13 macaques included in our study were anesthetized with isoflurane (concentration range 0.95–1.5%) and mechanically ventilated.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Nine macaque fMRI runs (from 7/13 subjects) had a single prominent asymmetric PC (median r>0.15).
source: We selected nine runs (from 7/13 subjects) with a single prominent asymmetric PC (median r>0.15) and used these PCs as regressors for GLM.
evidence: This describes the data selection for analysis.

claim: The macaque group statistical map exhibited striking homology with the human burst-suppression map.
source: The group statistical map (Figure 3C–E) exhibited striking homology with the human burst-suppression map.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing species.

claim: In macaques, significantly correlated areas with burst-suppression included the striatum and most of the cortex, with exceptions including V1, extrastriate visual areas, parts of somatosensory and motor cortices on either side of the central sulcus, the subcallosal cortex, and the parahippocampal gyrus.
source: Significantly correlated areas included the striatum and most of the cortex, with the following exceptions: V1, extrastriate visual areas, parts of somatosensory and motor cortices on either side of the central sulcus, the subcallosal cortex, and the parahippocampal gyrus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the macaque group-level analysis.

claim: One notable difference between macaque and human maps was the auditory cortex, the entirety of which was among the positively correlated areas in macaques.
source: One notable difference to the human map was the auditory cortex, the entirety of which was among the positively correlated areas.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between species.

claim: The cerebellar cortex was not correlated with burst-suppression in macaques, while the thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala were partly involved.
source: The cerebellar cortex was not correlated with burst-suppression, while the thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala were partly involved (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the macaque group-level analysis.

claim: No significant anticorrelations were found around the ventricles or elsewhere in macaques.
source: No significant anticorrelations were found around the ventricles or elsewhere.
evidence: This is a data observation from the macaque analysis.

claim: Eight out of 20 marmoset subjects had a single prominent asymmetric PC (median cortex-wide r>0.22).
source: We selected 8/20 subjects with a single prominent asymmetric PC (median cortex-wide r>0.22) and used these PCs as GLM regressors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes the data selection for marmoset analysis.

claim: The marmoset group statistical map was functionally homologous to the macaque map.
source: The resulting map (Figure 4C–E) was functionally homologous to the macaque map.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing species.

claim: In marmosets, positively correlated areas with burst-suppression comprised the striatum and a large part of the cortex—including auditory areas, but excluding V1, extrastriate visual areas, parts of somatosensory and motor cortices, and most of the parahippocampal gyrus.
source: Positively correlated areas comprised the striatum and a large part of the cortex—including auditory areas, but excluding V1, extrastriate visual areas, parts of somatosensory and motor cortices, and most of the parahippocampal gyrus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the marmoset group-level analysis.

claim: The cerebellar cortex and the thalamus (except for a small anterior part) were not correlated with burst-suppression in marmosets, while the hippocampus and the amygdala were correlated with it in parts.
source: The cerebellar cortex and the thalamus (except for a small anterior part) were not correlated with burst-suppression, while the hippocampus and the amygdala were correlated with it in parts (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the marmoset group-level analysis.

claim: No significant anticorrelations were found in marmosets.
source: No significant anticorrelations were found.
evidence: This is a data observation from the marmoset analysis.

claim: In one additional marmoset with whole-brain fMRI coverage, all four fMRI runs exhibited asymmetric PCs.
source: To ensure that the entirety of V1 was uncorrelated with asymmetric PCs, we obtained fMRI data with whole-brain coverage from one additional marmoset (four fMRI runs, each lasting 5 min, acquired at an isoflurane concentration of 1.1%). All four fMRI runs exhibited asymmetric PCs, which were used to compute a map via a fixed-effects GLM analysis.
evidence: This describes additional data collection and analysis.

claim: The whole-brain marmoset map showed lack of correlation across V1, including the posterior parts that were previously excluded from the field of view.
source: The map showed lack of correlation across V1, including the posterior parts that were previously excluded from the field of view (see Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a data observation confirming the V1 exclusion.

claim: Several studies have identified burst-suppression in electrophysiological recordings of rats anesthetized with isoflurane, mostly at concentrations between 1.3 and 2%.
source: Several studies have identified burst-suppression in electrophysiological recordings of rats anesthetized with isoflurane, mostly at concentrations between 1.3 and 2% (Detsch et al., 2002; Hudetz and Imas, 2007; Liu et al., 2011; Masamoto et al., 2009; Stenroos et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: One study described the potential fMRI correlate of burst-suppression in rats as widespread BOLD synchrony across the cortex and the striatum.
source: One study described the potential fMRI correlate of burst-suppression in rats: widespread BOLD synchrony across the cortex and the striatum (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of a previous study supported by a citation.

claim: Multiple asymmetric PCs were found across all rat fMRI runs.
source: We found multiple asymmetric PCs across all fMRI runs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a data observation from the rat analysis.

claim: 28 rat fMRI runs were selected for analysis (24 acquired at 2% isoflurane and 4 at 1.5%).
source: To select the ones most resembling burst-suppression, we focused on the subset of runs containing at least one asymmetric PC with median cortex-wide r>0.2 (37/64) but excluded nine runs that also had a second PC with relatively high median r value (within r=0.15 of the most asymmetric PC). We were left with 28 runs, 24 of which were acquired at 2% isoflurane and 4 at 1.5%.
evidence: This describes the data selection for rat analysis.

claim: The rat group-level statistical map showed significant correlation with the asymmetric PCs in the striatum and the entire neocortex.
source: The map (Figure 5C–E) showed significant correlation with the asymmetric PCs in the striatum and the entire neocortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the rat group-level analysis.

claim: Contrary to primates, the rat burst-suppression map included all primary sensory and motor cortices.
source: Contrary to primates, the map included all primary sensory and motor cortices.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing rats to primates.

claim: The cerebellar cortex and the amygdala did not correlate with burst-suppression in rats, while significant correlations were found in parts of the thalamus (medial) and the hippocampus.
source: The cerebellar cortex and the amygdala did not correlate with burst-suppression, while significant correlations were found in parts of the thalamus (medial) and the hippocampus (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the rat group-level analysis.

claim: No significant anticorrelations were found in rats.
source: No significant anticorrelations were found.
evidence: This is a data observation from the rat analysis.

claim: The rat burst-suppression map resembles a unified cortico-striatal network often found by BOLD fMRI studies in isoflurane-anesthetized rats.
source: The burst-suppression map shown in Figure 5 resembles a unified cortico-striatal network often found by BOLD fMRI studies in isoflurane-anesthetized rats (Kalthoff et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2011; Paasonen et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2010), suggesting that previous studies were potentially conducted during burst-suppression.
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations, leading to an inference.

claim: A single asymmetric PC (median cortex-wide r>0.2) was found in all rats from the Rat 2 dataset (Paasonen et al., 2018).
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5, we found a single asymmetric PC (median cortex-wide r>0.2) in all rats, with spatial distribution that matched both the unified network described in the original study (Paasonen et al., 2018) and the rat burst-suppression map in the present manuscript.
evidence: This is a data observation from reanalysis of a previous dataset.

claim: The results strongly suggest that the apparent unification of cortex and striatum into a single functional network is a direct effect of burst-suppression.
source: The results strongly suggest that the apparent unification of cortex and striatum into a single functional network is a direct effect of burst-suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis.

claim: The main inter-species difference was the exclusion of visual areas (and parts of other unimodal cortices) in primates, but not in rats.
source: The main inter-species difference was the exclusion of visual areas (and parts of other unimodal cortices) in primates, but not in rats.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary comparative finding.

claim: The sparing of V1 in primates cannot be attributed to a fluke of thresholding or to regional differences in temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR).
source: This finding cannot be attributed to a fluke of thresholding (see unthresholded T statistic maps in figure supplement 3 of Figures 2—5) or to regional differences in temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR, see figure supplement 4 of Figures 2—5).
evidence: This addresses potential confounds with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Other macaque brain areas with comparably low tSNR values, such as area TE of the inferior temporal cortex, were significantly correlated with asymmetric PCs.
source: Other macaque brain areas with comparably low tSNR values, such as area TE of the inferior temporal cortex, were significantly correlated with asymmetric PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a data observation that rules out tSNR as the sole explanation for V1 exclusion.

claim: V1 activity in rats was indistinguishable from that of the cingulate across all metrics: BOLD signal amplitude (p=0.63), PSD, and seed-based correlation map.
source: V1 activity in rats was indistinguishable from that of the cingulate across all metrics: BOLD signal amplitude (p=0.63, paired samples two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), PSD, and seed-based correlation map.
evidence: This is a quantitative data observation from the region-of-interest analysis.

claim: V1 activity in primates was very different from the cingulate: BOLD signal amplitude was reduced (p<0.001 in humans, p=0.004 in macaques, p=0.008 in marmosets), PSD was lower across all frequencies, and seed-based correlation maps were confined to the V1 itself.
source: Conversely, V1 activity in primates was very different from the cingulate: BOLD signal amplitude was reduced (p<0.001 in humans, p=0.004 in macaques, p=0.008 in marmosets; paired samples two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), PSD was lower across all frequencies, and seed-based correlation maps were confined to the V1 itself, barely extending beyond the seed borders.
evidence: This is a quantitative data observation from the region-of-interest analysis.

claim: Three possible mechanisms for the apparent uncoupling of V1 in primates are: V1 is engaged in continuous slow waves without suppressions, it is in constant suppression, or there is a local change in neurovascular coupling.
source: We can conceive three possible mechanisms for the apparent uncoupling of V1 in primates: V1 is engaged in continuous slow waves without suppressions, it is in constant suppression, or there is a local change in neurovascular coupling.
evidence: This presents possible explanations for the observed phenomenon.

claim: In the previous analysis of the human dataset, the occipital electrodes of the EEG showed the same bursts as the more anterior electrodes.
source: In the previous analysis of the human dataset (Golkowski et al., 2017), the occipital electrodes of the EEG showed the same bursts as the more anterior electrodes, which might imply a true uncoupling between the electrical activity and the BOLD signal in V1.
evidence: This is an observation from a previous study, cited here.

claim: EEG may lack the spatial resolution to record a different electrical activity originating in V1.
source: However, EEG may simply lack the spatial resolution to record a different electrical activity originating in V1: the small V1 area on the lateral cortical surface is dwarfed by non-visual areas engaging in burst-suppression (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the EEG observation.

claim: In 12 human subjects, both V1 and cingulate exhibited a reduction in BOLD signal amplitude from low to intermediate sevoflurane concentrations.
source: In summary, both V1 and cingulate exhibited a reduction in BOLD signal amplitude from low to intermediate concentrations.
evidence: This is a data observation from the analysis of sevoflurane concentration effects.

claim: During the high sevoflurane concentration (burst-suppression), the signal amplitude rose significantly in cingulate, but stayed the same as during the intermediate concentration in V1.
source: During the high concentration (burst-suppression), the signal amplitude rose significantly in cingulate, but stayed the same as during the intermediate concentration in V1—albeit with a slight shift toward lower frequencies.
evidence: This is a data observation from the analysis of sevoflurane concentration effects.

claim: Assuming the presence of continuous slow waves in V1 during the intermediate concentration, they are likely sustained through the high concentration as well.
source: Assuming the presence of continuous slow waves in V1 during the intermediate concentration, they are likely sustained through the high concentration as well.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: In case of a complete suppression of slow-wave activity in V1, a noticeable further reduction in BOLD signal amplitude would be expected.
source: In case of a complete suppression of slow-wave activity, a noticeable further reduction in BOLD signal amplitude would be expected.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected under a different scenario.

claim: A local change in neurovascular coupling in V1, though unlikely, cannot be ruled out with the current data.
source: A local change in neurovascular coupling, though unlikely, cannot be ruled out with the current data.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the interpretation of the data.

claim: The threshold for PC asymmetry (median cortex-wide r) is arbitrarily defined, which constitutes a weakness.
source: The threshold for PC asymmetry (median cortex-wide r) is arbitrarily defined, which constitutes a weakness, since the appropriate value is expected to vary depending on animal species, anesthetic agent, and imaging parameters.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: The isoflurane concentration range at which asymmetric PCs were detected closely matches previous reports of burst-suppression in macaques and rats.
source: First, the isoflurane concentration range at which these asymmetric PCs were detected closely matches previous reports of burst-suppression in macaques (Vincent et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2019) and rats (Detsch et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2011; Masamoto et al., 2009; Stenroos et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a validation of the method through comparison with previous literature.

claim: Almost all asymmetric PCs in rats were found at a concentration of 2% isoflurane and less so at 1.5 or 2.5%.
source: In this regard, our findings in rats are especially encouraging, because almost all asymmetric PCs were found at a concentration of 2% and less so at 1.5 or 2.5% (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a data observation supporting the validity of the method.

claim: The detected widespread fluctuations cannot be attributed to known non-neural sources, such as physiology or motion.
source: Second, the detected widespread fluctuations cannot be attributed to known non-neural sources, such as physiology or motion.
evidence: This is an inference ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: The asymmetric PCs displayed quasi-periodicity and were overwhelmingly correlated with gray matter areas.
source: The asymmetric PCs displayed quasi-periodicity and were overwhelmingly correlated with gray matter areas.
evidence: This is a data observation supporting the neural origin of the signal.

claim: Physiological noise related to mechanical ventilation or heartbeat would have been strictly periodic, while motion artifacts are known to distribute along image edges.
source: Physiological noise related to mechanical ventilation or heartbeat would have been strictly periodic, while motion artifacts are known to distribute along image edges.
evidence: This is reasoning based on known characteristics of artifacts.

claim: All evidence points toward burst-suppression as the underlying cause of the selected asymmetric PCs in the investigated animals.
source: In summary, all evidence points toward burst-suppression as the underlying cause of the selected asymmetric PCs in the investigated animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The method should not be viewed as an automated fMRI-based classification of burst-suppression but instead as a heuristic algorithm for identifying this state.
source: Given the arbitrary threshold limitation, our method should not be viewed as an automated fMRI-based classification of burst-suppression but instead as a heuristic algorithm for identifying this state.
evidence: This is a clarification of the method's scope and limitations.

claim: Animal fMRI researchers could use the algorithm to screen datasets for the presence of burst-suppression.
source: Animal fMRI researchers could use the algorithm to screen datasets for the presence of burst-suppression—as we did in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the method.

claim: The generalization of the method to other animal species and anesthetic agents warrants caution, keeping in mind that the amplitude and duration of bursts vary across anesthetics.
source: That said, the generalization of the method to other animal species and anesthetic agents warrants caution, keeping in mind that the amplitude and duration of bursts vary across anesthetics (Akrawi et al., 1996; Fleischmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a cautionary note about the method's limitations, supported by citations.

claim: One potential clinical application concerns the management of comatose patients, where burst-suppression is often present.
source: One potential clinical application concerns the management of comatose patients, where burst-suppression is often present—either transiently or throughout (Brenner, 1985; Brown et al., 2010; Cloostermans et al., 2012; Hofmeijer et al., 2014; Young, 2000).
evidence: This is a proposed application supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: After appropriate validation, the method could map burst-suppression in comatose patients, even at centers lacking the capacity for simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings.
source: After appropriate validation, our method could map burst-suppression in these patients, even at centers lacking the capacity for simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings.
evidence: This is a proposed application with a caveat about validation.

claim: An fMRI readout of burst-suppression, with its high spatial resolution and whole-brain coverage, could provide clinicians with information inaccessible by EEG.
source: An fMRI readout of burst-suppression, with its high spatial resolution and whole-brain coverage, could provide clinicians with information inaccessible by EEG.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical utility.

claim: The apparent exclusion of V1 from burst-suppression replicates the previous analysis in humans.
source: The apparent exclusion of V1 replicates the previous analysis in humans (Golkowski et al., 2017) and corroborates an existing report in macaques (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a validation of the finding through comparison with previous studies.

claim: The macaque map constitutes an important generalization, as it is based on seven long-tailed macaques—compared with only two rhesus individuals in the previous study.
source: Still, our macaque map constitutes an important generalization, as it is based on seven long-tailed macaques—compared with only two rhesus individuals in the previous study.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the current study.

claim: The marmoset burst-suppression map is, to our knowledge, the first of its kind and suggests that V1 exclusion may be a general primate feature.
source: The marmoset burst-suppression map is, to our knowledge, the first of its kind and suggests that V1 exclusion may be a general primate feature.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding and an inference about its generality.

claim: The pancortical distribution of burst-suppression in rats agrees with all previous findings in this species by fMRI or calcium imaging.
source: The pancortical distribution of burst-suppression in rats agrees with all previous findings in this species by fMRI (Aedo-Jury et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2011; Paasonen et al., 2020; Schwalm et al., 2017) or calcium imaging (Ming et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a validation of the finding through comparison with previous literature.

claim: The strength of the approach lies in computing all maps with the same data-driven approach, thus allowing direct cross-species comparisons.
source: The strength of our approach lies in computing all maps with the same data-driven approach, thus allowing us to make direct cross-species comparisons.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Recent work describes bursts as complex waves emerging from a spatially shifting focus and rapidly spreading through the cortex.
source: While bursts were traditionally viewed as synchronous cortex-wide events, recent work rather describes them as complex waves (Bojak et al., 2015) emerging from a spatially shifting focus and rapidly spreading through the cortex (Ming et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of recent research supported by citations.

claim: Electrocortical recordings in propofol-anesthetized human patients revealed that some electrodes could display continuous activity while others engaged in burst-suppression.
source: Electrocortical recordings in propofol-anesthetized human patients revealed that some electrodes could display continuous activity while others engaged in burst-suppression (Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of a previous study supported by a citation.

claim: Together with our results, this implies that brain areas may vary in their propensity for generating and/or propagating bursts.
source: Together with our results, this implies that brain areas may vary in their propensity for generating and/or propagating bursts.
evidence: This is an inference combining the current results with previous findings.

claim: Regional metabolic differences could underlie variability in burst propensity, according to a proposed neurophysiological-metabolic model of burst-suppression.
source: Regional metabolic differences could underlie such variability, according to a proposed neurophysiological-metabolic model of burst-suppression (Ching et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on a cited model.

claim: This model posits that suppressions occur when metabolic resources can no longer sustain neuronal firing, whereas bursts constitute transient recoveries of activity—enabled by slow metabolic replenishment.
source: This model posits that suppressions occur when metabolic resources can no longer sustain neuronal firing, whereas bursts constitute transient recoveries of activity—enabled by slow metabolic replenishment.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical model from the cited literature.

claim: The visual cortex of primates could impose special metabolic demands and thus find itself at an extreme end of the spectrum for burst propensity.
source: The visual cortex of primates could impose special metabolic demands and thus find itself at an extreme end of the spectrum for burst propensity.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed V1 exclusion.

claim: Such special demands could arise from the visual cortex's many distinctive characteristics—including cytoarchitecture, neurotransmitter receptor expression, functional connectivity profile, and cortical myelin density.
source: Such special demands could arise from its many distinctive characteristics—including cytoarchitecture, neurotransmitter receptor expression (Froudist-Walsh et al., 2021), functional connectivity profile (Margulies et al., 2016), and cortical myelin density (Van Essen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Many areas excluded from primate burst-suppression maps—V1, MT, primary motor, and somatosensory cortices—are among the richest in myelin.
source: We particularly suspect cortical myelin to play a role, considering that many areas excluded from our primate burst-suppression maps—V1, MT, primary motor, and somatosensory cortices—are among the richest in myelin (Van Essen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Rodents exhibit a more uniform myelin distribution, which could translate in a likewise uniform propensity for bursting.
source: Conversely, rodents exhibit a more uniform myelin distribution (Fulcher et al., 2019), which could translate in a likewise uniform propensity for bursting.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: The non-correlation of V1 and other primary sensory areas with burst-suppression challenges existing ideas about the origin of bursts.
source: Whatever the cause, the non-correlation of V1 and other primary sensory areas with burst-suppression challenges existing ideas about the origin of bursts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the findings.

claim: Studies in isoflurane-anesthetized humans, cats, rats, and mice showed that bursts can be evoked by incoming sensory stimuli, including flashes of light.
source: Studies in isoflurane-anesthetized humans, cats, rats, and mice showed that bursts can be evoked by incoming sensory stimuli, including flashes of light (Hartikainen et al., 1995; Hudetz and Imas, 2007; Kroeger and Amzica, 2007; Land et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: Burst-suppression has been described as a state of cortical hypersensitivity, during which even subliminal sensory stimuli can trigger a burst excitation.
source: Consequently, burst-suppression has been described as a state of cortical hypersensitivity, during which even subliminal sensory stimuli can trigger a burst excitation (Kroeger and Amzica, 2007).
evidence: This is a description of a concept from the cited literature.

claim: In that case, bursts would be expected to originate at the stimulated sensory area and then spread throughout the cortex indiscriminately, like ripples on a pond.
source: In that case, bursts would be expected to originate at the stimulated sensory area and then spread throughout the cortex indiscriminately, like ripples on a pond (Muller et al., 2018; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Schwalm et al., 2017; Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a logical expectation based on the cited literature.

claim: The pancortical rodent map is fully compatible with the view of bursts spreading like ripples on a pond.
source: The pancortical rodent map is fully compatible with this view, but the exclusion of sensory areas in primates seems paradoxical: why would the areas of origin not be a part of the ripple?
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in relation to existing models.

claim: The exclusion of sensory areas in primates seems paradoxical: why would the areas of origin not be a part of the ripple?
source: The pancortical rodent map is fully compatible with this view, but the exclusion of sensory areas in primates seems paradoxical: why would the areas of origin not be a part of the ripple?
evidence: This is a question raised by the findings, highlighting a paradox.

claim: A possible explanation is that the bursts captured in the data were internally generated or evoked through a non-excluded sensory modality (e.g., auditory areas in non-human primates).
source: A possible explanation is that the bursts captured in our data were internally generated or evoked through a non-excluded sensory modality (e.g., auditory areas in non-human primates).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed paradox.

claim: A closer investigation of sensory-evoked bursts in primates is warranted—especially with visual stimuli.
source: Nevertheless, a closer investigation of sensory-evoked bursts in primates is warranted—especially with visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: The striatum displayed the strongest correlation with burst-suppression across all four species—showing that the cortex does not act in isolation.
source: Among these, the striatum displayed the strongest correlation with burst-suppression across all four species—showing that the cortex does not act in isolation.
evidence: This is a data observation and its interpretation.

claim: Cortico-striatal loops may play an important—but yet unexplored—role in burst propagation.
source: Cortico-striatal loops may play an important—but yet unexplored—role in burst propagation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: The thalamus was only partly correlated with burst-suppression, and to a varying extent across species.
source: The thalamus, on the contrary, was only partly correlated with burst-suppression, and to a varying extent across species.
evidence: This is a data observation from the study.

claim: Anteromedial parts of the thalamus were more likely to be involved than posterolateral parts, possibly reflecting a differential role played by thalamic primary relay centers and higher-order nuclei.
source: Interestingly, anteromedial parts were more likely to be involved than posterolateral parts, possibly reflecting a differential role played by thalamic primary relay centers and higher-order nuclei, as previously hypothesized (Ming et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a data observation and a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Regional variations in thalamic activity could even shape cortical differences since the thalamus may be important for driving burst onsets.
source: Regional variations in thalamic activity could even shape cortical differences since the thalamus may be important for driving burst onsets (Ming et al., 2020; Steriade et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Similar to the thalamus, the hippocampus and amygdala were partially correlated with burst-suppression.
source: Similar to the thalamus, the hippocampus and amygdala were partially correlated with burst-suppression.
evidence: This is a data observation from the study.

claim: In primates, the hippocampus and amygdala are located in low signal-to-noise areas and often suffer from susceptibility-induced distortions.
source: However, we refrain from concrete conclusions, since in primates, these two structures are located in low signal-to-noise areas and often suffer from susceptibility-induced distortions (see figure supplement 4 of Figures 2—5).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a technical limitation affecting interpretation.

claim: The non-correlation of the cerebellar cortex with burst-suppression is likely a true effect, given its consistency across all species.
source: Nevertheless, the non-correlation of the cerebellar cortex with burst-suppression is likely a true effect, given its consistency across all species.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on consistency across species.

claim: Several rodent studies may refer to burst-suppression as 'slow oscillation'—meaning a<1 Hz alternation between a depolarized 'UP' state of neural activity and a hyperpolarized 'DOWN' state of silence.
source: It has been pointed out (Ming et al., 2020) that several rodent studies may refer to the same phenomenon as 'slow oscillation' (Aedo-Jury et al., 2020; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Schwalm et al., 2017; Stroh et al., 2013)—meaning a<1 Hz alternation between a depolarized 'UP' state of neural activity and a hyperpolarized 'DOWN' state of silence (Steriade and Nunez, 1993).
evidence: This is a clarification of terminology supported by citations.

claim: In the slow oscillation context, suppressions can be viewed as prolonged DOWN states.
source: In the slow oscillation context, suppressions can be viewed as prolonged DOWN states (Ching et al., 2012; Kroeger and Amzica, 2007).
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The line between slow oscillation and burst-suppression is blurry, given the gradual dose-dependent lengthening of quiescent periods.
source: However, the line between the two is blurry, given the gradual dose-dependent lengthening of quiescent periods.
evidence: This is an observation about the difficulty in distinguishing the two phenomena.

claim: Bursts and suppressions alternate faster when moving from humans to non-human primates to rats.
source: We noticed that bursts and suppressions alternate faster when moving from humans to non-human primates to rats (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a data observation from the study.

claim: Within the framework of the neurophysiological-metabolic model of burst-suppression, differences in timescale could reflect the faster metabolic rate of smaller animals.
source: Within the framework of the neurophysiological-metabolic model of burst-suppression (Ching et al., 2012), such differences in timescale could reflect the faster metabolic rate of smaller animals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on a cited model.

claim: Verifying the hypothesis about metabolic rate and burst timescale would require further studies involving direct neural recordings.
source: Verifying this hypothesis would require further studies involving direct neural recordings.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: A caveat concerning the cross-species comparison is that the depth of anesthesia was not standardized across species.
source: A caveat concerning our cross-species comparison of burst-suppression maps and timescales might be that the depth of anesthesia was not standardized across species.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: In humans, the highest sevoflurane concentration led to burst-suppression, with suppressions occupying roughly 50% of the time.
source: In humans, the highest sevoflurane concentration led to burst-suppression, with suppressions occupying roughly 50% of the time.
evidence: This is a data observation from the human study.

claim: In rats, burst-suppression was most reliably produced at the intermediate concentration of 2% isoflurane, while the 2.5% concentration probably corresponded to a near-constant isoelectric state.
source: In rats, burst-suppression was most reliably produced at the intermediate concentration of 2% isoflurane, while the 2.5% concentration probably corresponded to a near-constant isoelectric state.
evidence: This is a data observation and interpretation from the rat study.

claim: The non-human primate studies did not involve graded levels of anesthetic concentration; the observed instances of burst-suppression were analyzed.
source: The non-human primate studies did not involve graded levels of anesthetic concentration; we rather analyzed the observed instances of burst-suppression.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for non-human primates.

claim: The non-human primate studies covered a wide age range, extending well into old age, which is expected to influence the concentration at which burst-suppression occurs since anesthetic requirements decrease with age.
source: An additional complication is that our non-human primate studies covered a wide age range (see Table 1), extending well into old age. This is expected to influence the concentration at which burst-suppression occurs since anesthetic requirements decrease with age (Nickalls and Mapleson, 2003).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a confounding factor supported by a citation.

claim: In future studies, it would be of interest to systematically assess the dose-dependent evolution of burst-suppression across species.
source: In future studies, it would be of interest to systematically assess the dose-dependent evolution of burst-suppression across species.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.
